We cut our AWS bill from Rs 4.2 lakh to Rs 1.6 lakh a month in 10 weeks. One change made things worse.

Disclosure: I'm the CTO of LogLantern, an open-source log viewer built in Bengaluru, and this is the bill for our hosted version. I'm sharing the cost work, not the product, so no link here.

TL;DR: Rs 4.2 lakh to Rs 1.6 lakh a month in 10 weeks. Most of it was boring stuff nobody had looked at since launch: network charges, log storage and servers sized for a load we never had. One "obvious" saving backfired, details below.

**Weeks 1-2: read the bill, cut nothing**

We spent two weeks only reading. Cost Explorer grouped by service told us very little. Grouped by usage type, it showed a big slice under "EC2-Other", which is where NAT gateway charges hide. Our services were reading logs from S3 through the NAT gateway and paying per GB processed for traffic that never needed to leave the VPC.

**What moved the number, biggest first**

1. S3 gateway endpoint. It's free, took about ten minutes of Terraform, and the NAT charge for S3 traffic disappeared. Largest single cut [saving: Rs X a month].
2. Right-sizing. Our query nodes were sized for a load test we ran once. After two weeks of CPU and memory graphs we dropped them a size and moved to Graviton [saving: Rs X].
3. Retention. Raw logs sat in S3 Standard forever. We added a lifecycle rule and a compaction job for older data [saving: Rs X].
4. Dev and staging off at night and on weekends. Dull, and nobody had ever done it [saving: Rs X].

Those, plus a few small ones, add up to the Rs 2.6 lakh a month we lost from the bill.

**The change that backfired**

To squeeze storage further I moved anything older than 7 days to Glacier Flexible Retrieval. On the spreadsheet it was a big saving. In real life people open a log viewer to look at last month's incident, not just last week's. The retrieval fees, the 90-day minimum storage charge and restores that take hours turned the saving into a pile of angry messages. We rolled it back to a plain 30-day rule into Standard-IA, which our users' query patterns can live with. I now check access patterns before I touch a storage class.

**What I'd do on day one next time**

Tag every resource by service, and set a budget alert at 70% of last month. We lost the first week guessing which service owned which line.

What was the first line item you found when you went through your own bill, and has an "obvious" saving ever cost you more than it saved?

OUTPUT PLAN (internal)
Source: Paisa Pe Charcha, 52-minute Hinglish episode, guest [Adviser name], SEBI-registered adviser. Idea: a 30-year-old should buy term insurance, not a ULIP.
1. Blog (English, 900 words): the reader's question "ULIP or term at 30?" with the answer first. CTA: listen to the full episode.
2. Carousel (Hinglish, 8 slides): five things to check before buying a ULIP. CTA: listen to the episode.
3. Reel A (Hinglish, 45 s): the bank-pitch moment, one idea: bundling hides what each part costs.
4. Reel B (Hinglish, 45 s): a different moment, one idea: size cover by who depends on you.
Quote check: every [exact quote, mm:ss] below must be pasted from the transcript word for word, and the adviser must OK any claim about money, before this goes out.

==================== 1. BLOG ====================

ULIP or term insurance at 30? Buy the cover first

Your bank's relationship manager has a plan for you. It's a ULIP, it gives you insurance and investment in one policy, and it costs Rs [X] a year. Your cousin says just buy term insurance. You are 30, you earn, and someone depends on that income. Which one comes first?

[Adviser name], a SEBI-registered adviser, answered this on Paisa Pe Charcha, a Mumbai personal-finance podcast. The answer for a 30-year-old: buy term insurance first and invest separately. Here is the reasoning, in the order a buyer needs it.

Who is hurt if your income stops?

Insurance exists for one situation. You die early, and your family still has a loan, school fees and monthly bills. A 30-year-old with a home loan or parents to support has the most to lose and the least saved.

A term plan does that one job. If you die during the term, your family receives the sum assured. If you live, it pays nothing back, and that is exactly why it is cheap.

[Adviser name] on why protection should stay protection: "[exact quote, mm:ss]"

What a ULIP is selling you

A ULIP bundles life cover with a market-linked investment. Part of each premium buys cover and part goes into funds you choose. It sounds efficient.

The catch is that one product now carries several charges: premium allocation, policy administration, mortality and fund management. The minimum lock-in is five years. Your policy's benefit illustration shows the actual charges and the life cover you are getting, so read that page before anything else.

Why bundling costs more than it looks

When protection and investment sit in one policy, you cannot see what either part costs. You cannot tell whether the cover is fairly priced, and you cannot tell whether the fund is competitive with one you could buy on its own.

You also lose flexibility. Your income, goals and risk appetite will change in five years. With two separate products you change one. With a ULIP you keep both or you exit both, and exiting early can mean extra charges.

[Adviser name] on bundling: "[exact quote, mm:ss]"

How much term cover, and for how long?

[Adviser name]'s sizing rule: [cover multiple or method, exactly as said in the episode, mm:ss].

A simple way to start is to add up three things: your outstanding loans, your family's yearly expenses, and the number of years until your youngest dependant can earn. Choose a term that ends around the age you plan to retire.

Where does the investing happen, then?

Separately, in whatever suits your goal and time horizon: a mutual fund SIP, PPF, your EPF. Keeping the two apart means you can stop, switch or top up one without touching the other. If you are unsure, talk to a SEBI-registered adviser, not to the person who earns a commission on the policy.

But I get nothing back from term insurance

This is the most common objection, and it is fair. A plain term plan returns nothing if you outlive it. That is the price of the low premium. The gap between a term premium and a ULIP premium is money you can invest on your own, in something you can see and change.

Some insurers sell term plans with return of premium. They cost more, so ask for both quotes and compare what you pay for the extra. Tax rules on insurance have also changed in recent years. They depend on premium size and policy date, so check the current rule before you count tax savings as a reason to buy.

Five questions to ask before you sign any ULIP

1. What is my sum assured, and how many times my annual premium is it?
2. What are all the charges, in rupees, in year 1, year 3 and year 5?
3. What will I get if I stop paying in year 3?
4. Which funds can I move between, and what does each switch cost?
5. Can you show me the benefit illustration in writing?

If the answers come slowly or vaguely, that tells you something too.

When could a ULIP still make sense?

[Adviser name]'s view on the exceptions: [one sentence from the episode, mm:ss]. If your situation looks like one of those, the same rule applies: read the charges and the lock-in before you sign.

Do this week

1. Write down your loans, your dependants and your household's yearly cost.
2. Get a term quote from at least two insurers and compare the claim settlement ratios each one publishes.
3. Answer the health, smoking and income questions honestly. A wrong answer can sink a claim later.
4. If you already hold a ULIP, do not surrender it in a hurry. Ask the insurer for the surrender value and charges first.

Credit and where to listen: this piece is based on Paisa Pe Charcha, episode [number], with [Adviser name], SEBI-registered adviser [registration number]. Listen to the full 52-minute episode: [link]. This is general education, not personalised advice.

==================== 2. INSTAGRAM CAROUSEL (Hinglish, 8 slides) ====================

Slide 1: 30 saal ke ho? ULIP kharidne se pehle ye 5 baatein padho.
Slide 2: ULIP = insurance + investment, ek hi policy mein. Sunne mein smart hai. Par ek product mein do kaam, matlab charges bhi kai.
Slide 3: Term insurance ka ek hi kaam hai: aapko kuch ho jaye to parivaar ko paisa mile. Isiliye premium kam rehta hai.
Slide 4: ULIP mein premium ka ek hissa cover mein jaata hai, baaki invest hota hai. Charges alag: allocation, admin, mortality, fund management.
Slide 5: ULIP ka lock-in kam se kam 5 saal ka hota hai. Beech mein chhodna mehenga pad sakta hai.
Slide 6: [Adviser name], SEBI-registered adviser, ki salah: pehle term cover lo, phir investment alag se karo. "[exact quote, mm:ss]"
Slide 7: Cover kitna? Loan, saal ka ghar-kharcha, aur kitne saal koi aap par nirbhar hai. Do insurers se quote lo.
Slide 8: Poora episode suno: Paisa Pe Charcha, episode [number], guest [Adviser name]. Link bio mein.

Caption:
ULIP ya term insurance: 30 saal ki umar mein pehle kya lein?
Swipe karke dekho ULIP ke charges mein kya chhup jaata hai. Short mein: pehle term cover, phir investment alag.
Guest: [Adviser name], SEBI-registered adviser, Paisa Pe Charcha. Sirf jaankari ke liye, personal salah nahi.
#TermInsurance #ULIP #PersonalFinance #PaisaPeCharcha

==================== 3. REEL A (45 s, Hinglish) ====================

0-3 s, hook (VO): Bank wale ne bola, ULIP lo, insurance bhi milega aur paisa bhi badhega. Ek minute ruko.
On-screen: ULIP ya term? 30 saal ki umar mein.

3-18 s (VO): ULIP mein ek policy ke andar do cheezein hoti hain, thoda cover aur thoda investment. Problem ye hai ki charges kai hain: allocation, admin, mortality, fund management. Aur alag se dikhta nahi ki cover kitne mein mil raha hai.

On-screen: Cover alag. Investment alag.

On-screen: Paisa Pe Charcha | Poora episode: link in bio | Sirf jaankari ke liye.

0-3 s, hook (VO): Agar aapki salary kal ruk jaye, to ghar kaun chalayega? Insurance ka sawaal yahin se shuru hota hai.
On-screen: Pehle sawaal, phir policy.

On-screen: 3 cheezein likho. 2 quote lo. Sach bharo.

[Tier-2 / metro] roles fill [X] days faster: what 18,400 blue-collar applications show

ShiftSathi studied 18,400 anonymised blue-collar job applications made on its platform between January and June 2026. We wanted to know which cities, shifts and pay bands get roles filled fastest. This post is written for HR heads at logistics and retail companies who hire at volume.

Why we looked at this
An open blue-collar role is a missed shift, a late delivery or an empty counter. That is why time to fill is the first number an operations head asks a hiring team for. Most companies know only their own average, so they cannot tell whether 18 days is good. These cuts give you an outside reference to compare against, by city group, shift and pay band.

Key findings
- Roles in [city group] were filled in a median of [X] days, against [Y] days in [city group] (n = [N] roles, [N] applications).
- [Shift] roles were filled [X] days [faster / slower] than [shift] roles (n = [N] roles).
- Roles in the [band] monthly pay band filled in [X] days, against [Y] days one band below (n = [N] roles).
- The fastest combination of city group, shift and pay band filled in [X] days. The slowest took [Y] (n = [N] roles each).

Methodology
Data: 18,400 job applications for blue-collar roles posted on the ShiftSathi platform from 1 January to 30 June 2026, covering [N] roles at [N] employers in [N] cities. Every record was anonymised before analysis. No name, phone number or address was used.
Days to fill: days from a role going live on ShiftSathi to the employer marking it filled. [Confirm definition.] We report medians, not averages, because a few slow roles distort the average.
Cleaning: we removed [N] duplicate applications and [N] roles that were withdrawn without a hire.
Groups: cities are grouped as [definition of metro and Tier-2 groups]. Shifts are [day / evening / night, with hours]. Pay bands are [band 1], [band 2] and [band 3], in Rs per month, as listed in the job post.
Limits: this is platform data, not the whole market. Employers who use ShiftSathi may differ from those who do not. We did not control for employer size or job type, so every difference below is an association, not proof of cause. Sponsor: none. [Confirm.]

Finding 1: [City group] roles filled [X] days faster than [city group] roles

[Chart 1: median days to fill by city group, n = [N] roles per group.]
Chart 1: [City group] roles filled in [X] days, [Y] days sooner than the slowest group.

The gap is [X] days at the median and [Y] days at the 90th percentile. Put plainly, the slow roles in [city group] were slower than most roles in [city group] were at all.

Why this might be so (our interpretation, not tested): [one hypothesis, for example a larger local pool of applicants per role, or fewer competing employers in the same area]. We saw [what the data shows for or against, with n].

What it means: if you hire in both groups, a single fill-time target for the whole network will be too tight for one group and too loose for the other. Set targets per city group.

Finding 2: [Shift] roles filled [X] days [faster / slower] than [shift] roles

[Chart 2: median days to fill by shift, n = [N] roles per shift.]
Chart 2: [Shift] roles took [X] days to fill, [Y] days [more / less] than [shift] roles.

[N]% of applications ([n] of 18,400) were for [shift] roles, yet [N]% of roles still open after [N] days were [shift] roles. [Add the one number that explains whether the problem is too few applicants or too many dropouts after applying.]

Why this might be so (our interpretation): [hypothesis, for example commute safety, transport at shift start or family constraints]. We did not ask applicants, so treat this as a question to test.

What it means: [shift] roles need a longer lead time. Open them [N] days earlier than the others.

Finding 3: Each step up in pay band cut fill time by [X] days, up to [band]

[Chart 3: median days to fill by pay band, n = [N] roles per band.]
Chart 3: Fill time fell from [X] days to [Y] days between the [band] and [band] pay bands, then flattened.

The change from [band] to [band] is worth [X] days. The change from [band] to [band] is worth [Y]. After [band], we saw no further gain (n = [N] roles).

Why this might be so (our interpretation): [hypothesis, for example candidates compare offers within a narrow range, so the lowest-paid roles lose out first].

What it means: a pay rise on a slow role may be cheaper than a vacancy. One open role costs [Rs X] a day in [lost orders or lost sales; employer's own figure]. Test raises on the slowest-filling roles first and measure the result.

Finding 4: The best and worst combinations are [X] days apart

[Chart 4: median days to fill for the 3 fastest and 3 slowest city-shift-pay combinations, n = [N] roles each.]
Chart 4: [City group], [shift], [band] roles fill in [X] days, and [city group], [shift], [band] roles take [Y].

No single factor explains the spread. [Describe which factor mattered most once the other two were held fixed, and the n behind each cell. Do not report any cell with fewer than [30] roles.]

Why this might be so (our interpretation): [hypothesis].

What it means: look at your own slowest combination, not at the network average. That is where a day saved is worth the most.

(Writer note: the brief supplies the design (two-season Maharashtra field trial, drip with plastic mulch versus furrow) and the two headline results (yield +18%, water use -31%) only. All three prior studies are visible [ref 1/2/3: authors, year, site, finding] placeholders with bracketed direction words, and every mechanism claim carries a bare [ref] for the author to fill; no study, author or number was invented. The only derived figure is the water-productivity ratio 1.18 / 0.69 = about 1.7, flagged in the text as simple division. Table numbers, season-wise p-values, site count, soil type, replication, harvest area, water-measurement method and the furrow schedule are [placeholders]. The three limitations are: two seasons at limited sites, drip and mulch confounded because they were tested as one treatment (this follows from the brief), and cost/plastic disposal not assessed (marked [confirm] because the brief does not say whether the trial assessed it). Discussion

Drip irrigation with plastic mulch raised onion bulb yield by 18% and reduced water use by 31% relative to furrow irrigation over two seasons of field trials in Maharashtra. Both changes were in the direction hypothesised and both appeared in each season (Table [n]; [season-wise p-values]). Dividing the two headline figures (1.18 / 0.69) indicates that water productivity under drip with mulch was roughly 1.7 times that under furrow irrigation. The measured water-productivity values are given in Table [n]. A yield gain that arrives together with a lower water bill is the combination that matters for onion growers in a state where irrigation water is scarce in the rabi season [ref].

The most likely explanation is that the two components of the treatment act on different losses. Drip delivers small, frequent applications to the root zone of a shallow-rooted crop such as onion, which limits deep percolation and keeps the soil moisture within a narrower band than furrow irrigation allows [ref]. Plastic mulch reduces evaporation from the soil surface and suppresses weeds, which would otherwise compete with a crop of poor competitive ability [ref]. Mulch also moderates soil temperature, which can affect bulb initiation and bulb size [ref]. We did not measure each of these pathways in this trial, so they remain explanations, not findings. [Add the one supporting observation from the trial, for example weed biomass or soil moisture readings, with its table reference.]

The yield response is [larger than / similar to / smaller than] that reported by [ref 1: authors, year, site, drip with mulch versus furrow, reported yield change of [X]%]. The difference may reflect [the most plausible reason from the paper, for example soil texture, cultivar or season length]. Our trial and [ref 1] agree on the direction of the effect, which strengthens confidence that the response is not specific to one site.

For water use, our saving of 31% is [within / above / below] the range of [X]% to [Y]% reported by [ref 2: authors, year, site, crop]. Reported savings depend heavily on how the furrow baseline is irrigated, because a furrow scheme that is already tightly scheduled leaves less to save. Our furrow plots were irrigated [schedule, as described in Methods], and the savings should be read against that baseline, not against farmers' practice in general.

[Ref 3: authors, year, site, finding on a related comparison, for example drip without mulch, or mulch in a different season] offers a useful contrast. They found [finding with number], whereas we found a combined effect of 18% on yield. Because our treatment combined drip and mulch, we cannot say how much of the gain belongs to each. If their result is representative, [one calibrated sentence on what it would imply for our split, using 'would suggest' or 'is consistent with']. A factorial design is needed to settle this.

The effect was present in both seasons, although its size differed ([season 1: yield +[X]%, water use -[Y]%]; [season 2: yield +[X]%, water use -[Y]%]). Some difference between seasons is expected, because rainfall, temperature and evaporative demand change the crop's water requirement and therefore how much any irrigation method can save [ref]. The season-by-treatment interaction was [significant / not significant] (p = [value]), so we report [pooled effects with season as a fixed factor / each season separately]. The agronomic meaning of the yield gain is also easier to judge in absolute terms: 18% on a furrow-irrigated mean of [X] t/ha is [Y] t/ha of additional bulbs, and 31% less water is [Z] mm per season.

Three limitations qualify these findings. First, the trial ran for two seasons at [one site / N sites] in Maharashtra, on [soil type]. The results may not transfer to other soils, climates or cultivars, and two seasons cannot capture the year-to-year variation in rainfall and temperature that growers face. Second, the comparison was drip with mulch against furrow irrigation, so the effects of drip and of mulch are confounded, as noted above. Third, [confirm: this trial did not assess] the cost of installing the drip system and laying the mulch, or the disposal of used plastic film. A yield gain does not establish a profit gain, and mulch residue is an environmental cost that a farm-level analysis would need to include.

The study also has strengths. The design was [randomised, with N replications per treatment], yield was measured from [harvest area] per plot, and water applied was [metered / calculated by method], not estimated from farmer recall. These features reduce the risk that the 18% and 31% differences arise from plot-level noise or measurement error.

Where groundwater is declining, a 31% reduction on every hectare may be worth more to a district than the yield gain alone [ref]. The yield and water figures here describe plots managed by a research team, and farm-level results are usually lower than trial results because of uneven management, so the on-farm gain should be confirmed before it is quoted as a promise to growers [ref]. For practice, the results support drip irrigation with plastic mulch as a way to produce more onions from less water under the conditions tested. For research, the next steps are a factorial trial that separates drip from mulch, a multi-site study across Maharashtra's onion-growing districts, and an economic analysis that includes capital cost and film disposal. In conclusion, drip irrigation with plastic mulch increased onion yield by 18% and reduced water use by 31% compared with furrow irrigation in this two-season trial. The evidence is consistent with a real agronomic benefit. That benefit should now be tested across sites and priced against its costs.

Published by KhataPay, Jaipur | Fieldwork July to August 2026 | [Month 2026]

Executive summary

The story in one paragraph
Accepting a digital payment and running a business on digital payments are different things. In our survey, [X]% of owners accept at least one digital method, but digital payments make up [Y]% of the median owner's monthly sales and [Z]% of what that owner pays out. This report measures where the gap sits, how it differs between Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities, and what owners say is holding it open. The figures are for the owners we surveyed, in the 14 cities we surveyed, and they should not be read as figures for all Indian MSMEs.

Key findings
1. [X]% of owners accept at least one digital payment method, and [Y]% accept UPI (n = 2,150). Implication: acceptance is [near saturation / still a gap], so the useful question for banks has moved from "do they accept?" to "how much of their sales comes through?".
2. Digital payments account for a median of [X]% of monthly sales, against [Y]% in cash (n = [N] owners who accept digital payments). Implication: [one line on what the median share means for settlement volumes per owner].
3. [X]% of owners pay most of their suppliers in cash (n = 2,150). Implication: supplier payments, not customer payments, are [the larger untouched flow / one more place to offer a digital option].
4. [X]% of owners say money from a digital sale takes more than [N] day(s) to arrive, and [Y]% see a failed or pending payment at least weekly (n = [N]). Implication: speed and reliability of settlement are [the first thing / not the first thing] an owner will judge a provider on.
5. Tier-3 owners earn [X] percentage points less of their sales digitally than Tier-2 owners ([Y]% against [Z]%; n = [N] and [N]). Implication: a single national playbook will miss [the tier with the larger gap].
6. [X]% of owners use their digital payment history when they apply for a loan, or say they would if asked (n = [N]). Implication: payment records are an asset owners already hold, and few lenders ask for them.
7. The most common barrier to accepting more digital payments is [barrier], named by [X]% of owners (multiple answers allowed; n = 2,150). Implication: [one line on who can remove this barrier].

What to do with these findings
Bank product heads: [one action tied to finding 4 or 5]. Journalists: findings 1, 3 and 5 can be quoted on their own with the sample description in the next section. Policy teams: [one action tied to finding 7].

Methodology

Who we asked
We surveyed 2,150 owners of micro, small and medium enterprises in 14 Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities. [N] respondents are in Tier-2 cities and [N] in Tier-3 cities. The cities are listed in Appendix A. An owner qualified if they run a business with [definition of MSME used, for example Udyam registration or turnover band] and take the decisions on payments.

What the survey covered
The questionnaire had five blocks. The first covered how the business is run: sector, size and years in operation. The others covered how customers pay, how the owner pays suppliers and staff, what happens when a payment fails or is delayed, and what the owner would need to use more digital payments. Each finding comes from one of these blocks, and the full report names the block under every finding.

How we asked
Fieldwork ran from [date] to [date] in July and August 2026, conducted by [fieldwork agency / KhataPay research team] through [mode: phone, face to face or online]. Respondents were recruited by [sampling method, for example quota sampling by city, sector and business size]. The interview took about [N] minutes and was available in [languages].

Weighting and margin of error
Results are [unweighted / weighted by city tier and business size to match [source]]. For the full sample of 2,150, the largest margin of error is about plus or minus 2.1 percentage points at 95% confidence, if the sample is treated as random. [Confirm with the fieldwork agency; delete this line if the sample was not probability-based.] Margins are wider for groups: a cut with [N] respondents carries a margin of about [X] points.

How to read the charts
Every chart shows its base (n). We show a segment only where it has at least [N] respondents. Differences between groups are given in percentage points, not percent. Money is in rupees, with lakh and crore used throughout; we do not mix in millions.

Sponsor and independence
KhataPay, a Jaipur fintech that provides digital payment and bookkeeping tools to MSMEs, funded and published this survey. KhataPay's own product does not appear in the findings. The questionnaire is in Appendix B so that readers can check how each question was worded.

Limits
These are self-reported answers, not transaction data, so owners may remember their share of sales imperfectly. The sample covers 14 cities and does not cover metros or rural areas. We did not control for sector, so a difference between cities may reflect a difference in the kind of business, not in the city. The findings describe association, not cause.

How to cite

ROSHNI ROOFTOP SOLAR: Telecalling script (Hinglish, Lucknow)

PRE-CALL NOTE (not spoken)
Who: a Lucknow homeowner who filled our Facebook rooftop-solar form. Check the lead source and consent on the CRM before dialling. Our guess: the summer bill hurts, and they worry about cost, subsidy and the roof. One goal for the call: a free site-survey slot with a date and time.

1. OPENER
"Namaste [naam] ji, main [caller name], Roshni Rooftop Solar, Lucknow se. Aapne Facebook par rooftop solar ke liye form bhara tha. Kya aapke paas do minute hain, kuch sawaal poochne ke liye?"
HAAN: go to Discovery. BAAD MEIN: "Kab call karun, aaj shaam ya kal subah?" Note the time and end the call. NA: "Theek hai, form dobara bharne ki zaroorat nahi. Dhanyavaad."

2. DISCOVERY (ask, then listen. Do not interrupt.)
Q1. "Aapka bijli ka bill mahine ka kitna aata hai? Garmi mein kitna chala jaata hai?"
Listen for: the summer figure. If the bill is below [minimum bill the client wants to qualify], say "Size thoda chhota banega, survey mein dekhenge." Then continue.
Q2. "Aapki chhat kaisi hai: pakki RCC ya tin shed? Aur kitni khuli jagah hai jahan din bhar dhoop aati hai?"
Listen for: shade, a water tank, a second floor planned.
Q3. "Ghar aapka apna hai, ya kiraye par?"
If rented: "Makaan malik se baat ho sakti hai? Unka number mil jaye to hum unse hi survey ka time le lenge."
Q4. "Aap kab tak lagwana chahte hain: is mahine, teen mahine mein, ya abhi sirf dekh rahe hain?"
Listen for: a deadline such as a summer peak, a loan, or a house under construction.

3. PITCH (about 40 words, say it slowly)
"Aapne bataya ki bill [X] aata hai. Rooftop solar se ye bill kam ho sakta hai, aur sarkari subsidy milti hai. Hum Lucknow mein [N] ghar kar chuke hain. Free survey mein hum chhat dekhkar likhit mein size aur kharcha batate hain."

4. OBJECTIONS (acknowledge, ask, answer, end with a question)
"Bahut mehenga hai."
"Sahi baat hai, shuruaat mein kharcha lagta hai. Aapke hisaab se kitna budget theek rahega? Survey ke baad aapko bill ke hisaab se size, kharcha aur subsidy likhit mein milegi. [Financing options, confirm with the client.] Kya hum pehle wo numbers dekh len?"

"Subsidy milti bhi hai ya nahi?"
"Aapka shak jayaz hai. Subsidy sarkari PM Surya Ghar scheme ki hai aur official portal par apply hota hai. Raashi system ke size par depend karti hai. Hum survey ke baad portal ke hisaab se exact amount batayenge. Kya main portal ka link WhatsApp par bhej dun, aap khud dekh lein?"

"Chhat se paani tapakne lagega."
"Ye darr aam hai. Panel chhat ke upar stand par lagte hain. Survey mein hum dekhte hain ki kahan lagana hai, aur wo tareeka aapko dikhate hain. [Mounting and sealing method, confirm with the installation team.] Aapki chhat par pehle kabhi paani tapka hai?"

"Soch ke bataunga."
"Bilkul sochiye. Bas ek baat bata dijiye: kis baat par sochna hai, kharcha, subsidy ya chhat? Survey free hai, aur uske numbers se soch-vichar aasan ho jaata hai. Kal shaam theek rahegi ya parso subah?"

"Quotation pehle se hai."
"Achhi baat hai, tulna karna samajhdari hai. Kis company ka quote hai? Hamare surveyor aapke quote ke panel, inverter aur warranty ko hamare numbers ke saath saath dikha sakte hain. Kya aap wo quote survey ke time dikha denge?"

5. CLOSE
"Survey ke do slot hain: [slot 1, for example kal shaam 5 baje] ya [slot 2, for example parso subah 11 baje]. Kaun sa theek rahega?"
After they pick: "Aapka address Lucknow mein kaun se area mein hai? Maine [din, date, samay] likh liya hai. WhatsApp par confirmation aayega, aur surveyor aane se pehle aapko call karega. Dhanyavaad."
Clear NO: "Theek hai, koi baat nahi. Agar baad mein mann badle, to is number par WhatsApp kar dijiye. Dhanyavaad."

6. IF NO ANSWER
Voicemail (about 40 words): "Namaste, main [caller name], Roshni Rooftop Solar, Lucknow se. Aapne Facebook par rooftop solar ke liye form bhara tha. Main aapko [time] par dobara call karunga. Jaldi baat karni ho to isi number par WhatsApp kar dijiye."
WhatsApp (about 40 words): "Namaste [naam] ji, main [caller name], Roshni Rooftop Solar se. Aapne rooftop solar ke liye form bhara tha. Free site survey kab theek rahega: kal ya parso? Bas 'Kal' ya 'Parso' likh dijiye."

Notes: You know these numbers better than I do. These are the two costs a transporter cannot easily pass on to the customer. Ask: which of the two hurt your margin more last year? Listen, and use their words on the next slide.

SLIDE 3 | The stakes
Headline: Every idle hour and detour is paid for in diesel you cannot bill
Body: Idle cost a month = trucks x idle hours a day x litres an hour x Rs per litre x 30. For [N] trucks, that is Rs [A] lakh a month.
Notes: Use their fleet size. Ask: roughly how many hours a day does a truck stand with the engine on, at loading, at the gate, at the dhaba? If they do not know, that is the point: without data, nobody does. Do the sum together and write the number on the slide.

SLIDE 4 | What good looks like
Headline: A good fleet knows its cost per kilometre, by truck, every morning
Body: By truck, by trip, by driver. Fuel, tolls, idle time and detention, each as one number, with yesterday's exceptions listed.
Notes: Your best operations manager does this in their head for ten favourite trucks. The goal is to do it for every truck, daily, without a spreadsheet. Ask: who prepares your cost per kilometre today, and how many days after month-end do you see it?

SLIDE 5 | How we get you there: see
Headline: You see every truck, trip and stop on one screen
Body: Live location, trip history and stop times for each truck. Plant and customer visits are marked on the map. [Screenshot: fleet map, trucks coloured by status.]
Notes: The outcome is fewer calls asking where the truck is. Show the live map. If they ask about devices and SIMs, point to slide 10.

SLIDE 6 | How we get you there: catch
Headline: You catch fuel leaks the same day, not at month-end
Body: Alerts for engine idling past [N] minutes, off-route driving and unplanned stops. Each alert names the truck, driver and place. [Screenshot: alert list.]
Notes: The outcome is lower idle and off-route fuel, tied to the number on slide 3. An alert read the next morning is worth more than a report read next month. Show one real alert if a client has allowed it.

SLIDE 7 | How we get you there: cost
Headline: You see tolls, fuel and waiting time as a cost per kilometre
Body: One daily report: cost per kilometre by truck and by route, with tolls, diesel and waiting time shown separately. [Screenshot: daily cost report.]
Notes: The outcome is knowing which route or truck loses money. Ask: which route do you suspect earns the least? We can test that in the pilot. [Confirm with product which cost lines the report shows without extra integration.]

SLIDE 8 | Who we are
Headline: RahiTrack tracks [N] trucks for [N] logistics companies from Gurugram
Body: [N] trucks live today. [N] fleet customers. Team of [N]. Support in [languages and hours].
Notes: One slide, kept short. We built RahiTrack for fleets of 200 to 2,000 trucks. At that size, watching every truck by phone stops working. Move on to the proof.

SLIDE 9 | Proof
Headline: [Client type] cut idle diesel by [X]% in [N] days
Body: [Client name, with permission]: [N] trucks, [N] routes. Idle fuel [X]% to [Y]%. Cost per kilometre Rs [A] to Rs [B]. Measured over [N] days against the [N] days before. "[Quote from the client's operations head, with permission]"
Notes: Tell the story: what they measured before, what they changed after the alerts, which number moved. Say how it was measured. If the buyer asks whether it will be the same for them, say the pilot decides that. It runs on their trucks, against a pass mark they set.

SLIDE 10 | How a pilot works
Headline: Your pilot trucks are live within [N] days of the go-ahead
Body: Days 1 to [N]: devices fitted on [N] trucks. Day [N]: your team is trained on the dashboard. Day 30: we review the results together.
Notes: Keep it concrete. Say who fits the devices, where, and how long each truck is off the road. [Confirm fitting process and downtime with the install team.] Answer the SIM and device questions here.

SLIDE 11 | Before we start
Headline: We agree the pass mark in writing before the first truck is fitted
Body: Three numbers against your previous 30 days: idle fuel, cost per kilometre, waiting hours. You set the pass mark for each. You provide [N] trucks, one operations contact and [trip and fuel data].
Notes: This makes the pilot easy to say yes to, because they define success. Do not suggest the pass mark. Ask: what drop in idle fuel would make this worth continuing?

SLIDE 12 | Next step
Headline: Let us run a 30-day pilot on [N] of your trucks from [date]
Body: You nominate one operations manager and [N] trucks. We fit, train and send a weekly summary. On day 30 we review with you and your finance head. Decision date: [date].
Notes: Ask for the yes in the room: shall we fix the start date today? If they need an approval, ask who gives it and put that conversation in the calendar before you leave. Send the one-page pilot plan the same day.

PRE-HEAD
For working women with PCOS who are tired of restarting a diet every Monday

HEADLINE
Cycle Reset: an 8-week plan to steady your energy and track your cycle with PCOS, without another crash diet

SUBHEAD
An online programme from Bengaluru nutritionist [Name], built around Indian meals, 30 minutes of movement a day and one simple cycle log. Next cohort starts Monday 16 November 2026.

[Button] Enrol in Cycle Reset: Rs 7,999

LEAD

It is 4:30 pm. Your laptop is open, your third chai has gone cold, and the afternoon crash has arrived right on time.

You promised yourself a proper lunch today. What you actually had was two biscuits from the pantry and a banana you ate standing up. Now your head is heavy, your hands want something sweet, and there are three hours of work left.

Tonight you will feel bad about it. You will tell yourself "kal se pakka". Tomorrow you will open the diet PDF from three Mondays ago, the one that said no roti, no rice, no sugar, no life, and you will try again. By Thursday, a client dinner or a late meeting will break it, and the whole plan will go into the same folder as the last one.

If this is you, nobody has to tell you that you are not lazy. You woke up early, you work a full day, you manage a house or a family WhatsApp group or both. You have tried a keto plan, a juice plan and a "PCOS diet" you found on Instagram. Some of them worked for a few weeks. None of them survived a normal week at your job.

This page is for you. It is about a different way to run the next eight weeks.

THE PROBLEM, AND WHAT IT COSTS YOU

PCOS is a hormonal and metabolic condition. It shows up differently in every woman: irregular cycles for one, tiredness and cravings for another, skin and hair changes for a third. Many women with PCOS also find that their body responds to meals, sleep and stress differently from their friends'. That is why the advice that works for your colleague can leave you worse off.

Most plans you find online treat PCOS as a weight problem and answer it with a deadline: lose this much by that date. A deadline plan has to be strict to hit the deadline. Strict plans cut meals, cut whole food groups, and demand time you do not have. When you slip, as anyone with a real job will, the plan has no way to take you back. You just feel you failed.

Here is what that costs, month after month. You lose energy at the same time every day and blame yourself. Your cycle does what it wants, and you cannot tell whether anything is helping because nothing is being tracked. Doctors' visits become a guessing exercise, because you cannot say what changed. And every restart makes the next one harder to believe in.

Lifestyle changes (food, movement, sleep) are the usual first step in PCOS care, and your doctor will likely say the same. The hard part has never been knowing that. The hard part is building a routine that holds up on a Tuesday when you have back-to-back calls and no time to cook.

WHY THIS WORKS WHEN THE CRASH DIETS DID NOT

The big idea behind Cycle Reset is one sentence: stop dieting at your PCOS and start running it like a routine.

A routine has three parts. Cycle Reset gives you all three, and keeps each one small enough to survive your week.

1. The Steady Plate. Four anchor meals a day built from food you already cook: dal, sabzi, roti or millets, curd, paneer, eggs if you eat them, sprouts, seasonal fruit. Each anchor meal has protein, fibre and a carbohydrate you choose. Nothing is banned. The aim is to stop the long gaps and the 4:30 pm crash, not to shrink your plate.

2. Small Movement. Thirty minutes a day, in pieces if you need to. A walk after lunch. A strength session you can do in a bedroom. A stretching routine for the days you are wrecked. You do not need a gym.

3. The Cycle Log. One page a day, under two minutes: energy out of 5, sleep, cycle day, any symptom. After a few weeks you stop guessing. You can see what a good day looks like for your body, and you have something concrete to show your gynaecologist or endocrinologist.

Crash diets try to change your body in a hurry. Cycle Reset changes your week. If a day goes wrong, the plan has a Reset Day. It is a short, simple way to get back on the routine the next morning, without paying for yesterday.

Cycle Reset does not treat or cure PCOS. Nothing on this page does. It gives you a way of eating, moving and tracking that you can stick to, and a log that helps you and your doctor see what is working.

[Testimonial slot 1: a real, named participant (first name, age, city, job) in her own words about energy or cycle tracking. Written consent on file. No weight figures. Placed here, before the price.]

WHO IS BEHIND IT

[Name] is a nutritionist in Bengaluru. [Qualification and registering body; years of practice; number of women worked with, only if it can be shown]. [Name] has built Cycle Reset around what working women actually tell her about their week. The meetings that run over. The tiffin that has to be packed in the morning. The festival sweets, the family dinner, the days with no energy to cook.

WHAT YOU GET

Everything below is included in the one price. Every item is there for a reason.

1. Eight weekly modules, each with a short video and a one-page plan, so you can do the week in 20 minutes of reading and watching.

WHAT EIGHT WEEKS LOOK LIKE

Weeks 1 and 2: set up your Steady Plate and your Cycle Log. No big changes yet; the first job is to see your own pattern.
Weeks 3 and 4: fix the long gaps between meals and add Small Movement. You start to see which meal sits right before your 4:30 pm crash.

WHAT A NORMAL DAY LOOKS LIKE

Here is a sample Week 3 weekday for an office-goer who eats vegetarian. Your own plan will differ, but the shape is the same.

7:30 am: Besan chilla with a spoonful of curd, plus a handful of roasted chana. Protein and fibre before the commute.
11:00 am: Fruit and a small handful of nuts at your desk. The aim is a shorter gap before lunch, which is where many afternoons start to go wrong.
1:30 pm: Two rotis (or a small bowl of millet), dal, sabzi, salad. Cooked the night before, packed in the tiffin.
5:00 pm: Chai if you like, with roasted makhana or sprouts chaat. Not biscuits.
8:30 pm: Paneer bhurji or moong dal khichdi with vegetables. Early enough that you are not eating at 10:30 pm.
Through the day: a 10-minute walk after lunch, a 20-minute strength track after work, and two minutes with the Cycle Log before bed.

None of this is fancy. It is food you already know, in an order that holds up on a busy day.

THE 30-DAY REFUND, IN PLAIN WORDS

What "follow the plan" means: you fill in your Cycle Log at least 5 days a week for the first 4 weeks. You also do the Week 1 to Week 4 meal and movement steps as written.

What "nothing improves" means: your own log, sent to us, shows no better energy scores and no clearer cycle pattern than you had in your first week. You decide, using your own numbers. We will not argue with them.

How to claim: email [support email] within 30 days of the cohort start date (by Wednesday 16 December 2026) with your Cycle Log attached. We refund within 7 working days.

This refund is about energy and cycle tracking. There is no guarantee about weight, and there will not be one, because PCOS does not work like that.

QUESTIONS WOMEN ASK BEFORE THEY ENROL

Is Cycle Reset a cure for PCOS?
No. PCOS does not have a cure, and anyone who says otherwise is selling you something. Cycle Reset is a lifestyle routine and a tracking habit to use alongside your doctor's advice.

Will I lose weight?
Some women do, some do not, and we do not promise it. The programme is built around energy and cycle tracking, not around a target weight.

I take medicines for PCOS. Do I stop them?
No. Keep taking whatever your doctor has prescribed. Show your doctor the plan and the Cycle Log before you start, especially if you have diabetes, thyroid problems or any other condition.

I do not have a PCOS diagnosis yet. Can I join?
Please see a gynaecologist or endocrinologist first. The programme is made for women who have a diagnosis or are already under a doctor's care for it. We cannot diagnose you.

I am vegetarian (or eggetarian, or Jain). Will the plan work?

I work 10-hour days, sometimes from home, sometimes in a hybrid office. Is there time?

What if I miss a week?
You use the Reset Day plan and pick up where you left. The weekly videos stay in your account, and the live calls are recorded.

Do I need a gym or special equipment?
No. The movement tracks use a mat and a chair. A walk counts.

I have tried everything and it never lasts. Why would this be different?
Most plans fail because they are built for a deadline and not for a Tuesday. This one is built for a Tuesday. Nothing is banned, there is a way back after a bad day, and you have someone to ask.

Can I do it with a friend or my sister?
Yes. Each person enrols separately so she gets her own intake review and her own plan.

Who is this not for?
Cycle Reset is not for you if you want a fast weight-loss plan or want to stop your medicines. If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, or have a history of an eating disorder, speak to your doctor before joining. Please speak to your doctor first, and write to [support email] if you are unsure.

CLOSE

The cohort runs from Monday 16 November to Sunday 10 January. You can spend those eight weeks the way you spent the last few attempts: a strict plan, a bad Thursday, and a quiet restart. Or you can spend them on a routine that fits a working day. You get a log that shows what your body is doing, and someone who replies when you write.

VYANG VAANI: 45-second reel script. "Pothole Adventure Park"

TARGET AND TRUTH (internal, not published)
Target: the city's municipal corporation and its yearly pre-monsoon promise of "pothole-free roads". A body with power and a budget, not a person. No individual is named anywhere.
Truth underneath: every May or June the corporation announces that roads will be repaired before the rains; every July the same roads carry potholes and the complaint line fills up. Source to link before posting: [the corporation's own pre-monsoon announcement or press note] and [its own pothole-complaint figures for the same year].
Voice rule: if the VO is AI-generated, say so in the caption. No real person's voice or face is imitated.

PREMISE
What if the potholes were not a failure but a tourist attraction, and the corporation advertised them as one?

SCRIPT

[0:00 - 0:05] STRAIGHT-FACED SETUP
Visual: drone-style shots of a rain-soaked city road, slow and golden, with calm travel-ad music.
VO (warm, slow, tourism-ad voice): Kya aap rozmarra ki zindagi se thak gaye hain? Aaiye, Pothole Adventure Park. Sheher ki sabse purani aur sabse zyada visit ki jaane wali attraction.
On-screen text 1: POTHOLE ADVENTURE PARK

[0:05 - 0:30] ESCALATION
Visual: scooters slowly dipping into water-filled craters; a car wheel disappearing; an auto bouncing.
VO: Yahan har saal naye rides add hote hain, aur sabse khaas baat, hamein inhe banana bhi nahi padta. Pehla ride: Deep Dive Zone, jahan aapki scooty ghutne tak paani mein jaati hai. Doosra: Free Back Adjustment, jahan har jhatke par aapki kamar ko chiropractor mil jaata hai. Teesra: Monsoon Mystery Box, ek pothole jo paani ke neeche chhupa hai. Aapko pata hi nahi chalega, kab aa gaya.
On-screen text 2: Entry free. Insurance aapki zimmedari.

[0:30 - 0:38] ESCALATION, THE TRUTH SHOWS
Visual: a man in a spotless shirt cuts a ribbon on a patch of dry road, then the camera pulls back to the same patch under water.
VO: Park ki maintenance? Woh har June mein ek press conference mein ho jaati hai.
On-screen text 3: Maintenance: har June, ek press conference

[0:38 - 0:44] PUNCHLINE
Visual: calm travel-ad close-up of a full pothole with the sun glinting on it.
VO: Humne vaada kiya tha ki sadkein monsoon se pehle theek ho jayengi. Humne yeh kabhi nahi kaha ki kaunse monsoon se pehle.

[0:44 - 0:45] TAG
Visual: a small plaque reading "Open all year."
VO: Ticket free hai. Aap tax de hi chuke ho.
On-screen text 4: Kaunsa monsoon? Tag karo [@municipal account]

LABEL (visible for the whole 45 seconds, top of frame, white text on a black strip)
SATIRE | Vyang Vaani | Yeh asli vigyapan nahi hai

VO word count: 137

CAPTION
Aapke sheher ka sabse popular park. Satire hai, par sadak asli hai. Apni sadak ka sabse favourite ride neeche tag karo, aur Nagar Nigam ko bhi. [@municipal account]
#VyangVaani #Satire #PotholeAdventurePark #Monsoon
